Secure blockchain based intrusion detection 
for IoT networks
Atul Kumar1, Bhisham Sharma2 and Ajit Noonia3*
1 Introduction

Abstract
A blockchain-enabled Model integrates blockchain technology with Intrusion 
Detection Systems to enhance the security of Internet of Things (IoT) networks. 
It ensures data integrity, decentralization, and tamper-proof logging of intrusion 
detection. The approach improves trust, transparency, and real-time threat detection 
in distributed IoT environments. The existing blockchain-based IDS approaches, 
Blockchain Enabled (BCE-IoT), uniquely integrate blockchain consensus with 
federated-style local training, lightweight cryptography, and Shapley Additive 
Explanations (SHAP)-based explainability, ensuring both security and interpretability 
in IoT environments. The proposed work combines Blockchain technology with 
explainable artificial intelligence solutions to create a new cybersecurity Model that 
strengthens intrusion detection within IoT networks. The proposed model enhances 
transparency in tracking cyberattacks by combining blockchain security storage 
capabilities with SHAP , an explainable AI. This research utilises machine learning and 
artificial intelligence to detect threats in real-time, countering Distributed Denial of 
Service (DDoS), Denial of Service (DoS), scanning, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), injection, 
password, and backdoor attacks. BCE-IoT delivers more precise security by combining 
blockchain’s permanent data features and AI anomaly detectors, thereby reducing 
security alert mistakes. The performance effectiveness of Blockchain-Enabled IoT 
surpasses that of the Content Integrity Detection System. It combines Blockchain 
and Software-Defined Networking to enhance security in network environments, 
utilising blockchain-based mutual confirmation for software-defined networking to 
detect and block cyber threats. The evaluation establishes BCE-IoT as an effective 
IoT network security solution that delivers strong cybersecurity features, is adaptable 
to modern connected environments, and offers interpretable security solutions. The 
performance evaluations demonstrate that BCE-IoT provides a robust, flexible, and 
interpretable cybersecurity solution suitable for modern IoT environments.
Keywords Internet of things, Blockchain, Intrusion detection, Artificial intelligence, 
Software defined network, Distributed denial of service

The organizations are now demanding more interpretive machine learning models for 
cybersecurity applications, which has led to the growing complexity of system threats. 
SHAP is an advanced interpretability technique that reveals to users the decision-
making process of machine learning models. SHAP effects allow predictive outcome 
variables to become interpretable through SHAP analyses because the method applies 
game-theoretic concepts for distributing feature contributions towards predictions [ 2]. 
The multi-class split method enables SHAP to analyze multi-class classification data by 
providing separate SHAP value computations for every class, improving the interpreta -
tion of classification systems.
The construction of dependable interconnected systems depends on complete security

In this work, Blockchain is used not only as a tool of immutability but also to distrib -

recording intrusion incidents without tampering. Similarly, SHAP has been iteratively 
applied to multi-class intrusion detection, allowing for per-attack interpretability of fea -

These specific applications extend beyond ordinary blockchain and SHAP applications, 
directly enhancing the detection precision and reliability of BCE-IoT.
The effectiveness of the proposed BCE-IoT framework is evaluated using commonly 
used benchmarks, including accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and F1-score, to pro -
vide a comprehensive assessment of the detection performance.
To address these limitations, BCE-IoT introduces three novel design aspects: (i) inte -
gration of blockchain consensus with federated-style local training for decentralized 
trust management, (ii) use of XXTEA is also known as Tiny Encryption Algorithm 
(TEA) TEA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) to provide lightweight crypto -
graphic security for IoT devices, and (iii) SHAP-based explainability for enhanced 
interpretability. These features collectively distinguish BCE-IoT from prior blockchain-
enabled IDS frameworks.

2 Literature review

a Random Forest (RF) classifier to increase its detection rate. The team utilised three 
IoT-based datasets, namely NF-BoT-IoT-v2, NF-ToN-IoT-v2, and IoTDS20, as research 
input and modelled transparency using SHAPE methods. The accuracy of detection was 
significantly increased, as were precision, F1-scores, and recall values. The SHAP sys -
tem gave users clear explanations that displayed both model decisions and the essential

Despite these advancements, current research on intrusion detection still has signifi -
cant limitations. The majority of them are built on centralised architectures and hence 
they bring about single points of failure as well as scaling issues. Some of these mod -

identification of these gaps underscores the relevance of the proposed BCE-IoT model,

In summary, although previous IDS methods, including ensemble trees with SHAP ,

interpretability. To fill these gaps, the proposed BCE-IoT will combine blockchain con -
sensus, lightweight encryption, XXTEA, ECC, and SHAP-based explainability, thereby 
turning the solver into a more powerful and open IoT IDS.

3.1 NF-ToN-IoT-V2 dataset
The NF-ToN-IoT-V2 database contains 43 attributes focusing on packet size elements 
that researchers use to analyze network traffic patterns. Among the metrics are Total 
Length of Forward and Backward Packets and Max, Min, Mean, and Standard Devia -
tion measurements for both forward and backward packet lengths. A thorough analysis 
of network flow packet size distribution is derived from a set of features that include 
Max Packet Length, Min Packet Length, Packet Length Mean, Packet Length Standard 
Deviation, and Packet Length Variance. Network intrusion detection systems heav -
ily rely on packet size features because they enable the system to identify regular traf -
fic from malicious traffic patterns. The data completeness is evident in this dataset 
through the absence of missing values, while most features are distinct, except for one 
replicated description. Decentralized architecture ensures superior security and trust 
because it stays immune to tampering activities and fraud schemes. Blockchain technol -
ogy supports cybersecurity through threat detection and minimization of seven princi -
pal vulnerabilities, including Benign Scanning, as well as Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and 
Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks, Password Attacks and Injection Attacks, 
Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks, Backdoor Exploits, Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) 
Attacks, and Ransomware. Blockchain ensures secure digital transactions by leverag -
ing distributed ledger technology and strong encryption mechanisms, which collectively 
guard against unauthorized access, data tampering, and malicious activities. Table  1

3.2 Blockchain structure and security
A blockchain is programmed so that changing any earlier transaction is practically 
impossible due to its cryptographic defense system. The link between every block in the 
chain and the previous one, facilitated by a cryptographic hash, provides a tamper-proof 
format. As shown in Fig.  1, this linking establishes an immutable ledger where each 
transaction is securely recorded. The decentralized aspect of blockchain technology 
ensures that the ledger is not owned by a single entity but rather is distributed among 
various nodes within the network. In contrast to conventional centralized networks, 
where a single authority governs transactions, blockchain utilizes a consensus mecha -
nism to authenticate changes, making unauthorized alterations extremely challenging.

3.3 Steps for adding a new block
In order to add a new block B new with timestamp tnew to the existing blockchain, the fol-
lowing process is undertaken:
1. A new transaction is verified and approved by nodes on the network.
2. The approved transaction is included in a new block, Bnew, with its timestamp, tnew.
3. A cryptographic puzzle proof of work is created to append Bnew to the blockchain.
4. The new block is broadcast to all nodes for further verification and approval.
5. Once verified, Bnew is permanently added to the blockchain, ensuring its immutability:
BC := BC ∪{ (Bnew, tnew)} (2)
Through its design mechanism, blockchain protects its decentralized and tamper-proof 
nature, stabilizing cryptocurrency technologies, smart contracts, and cybersecurity 
applications.
A blockchain operates with a basic structure, as shown in Fig.  1, which shows a block 
design comprising transaction lists and header elements. The sequential chain of blocks 
derives its cryptographic security from the hash calculations performed on preceding 
header data, creating an immutable record. A block comprises two essential sections: 
the block header, which includes metadata of previous hashes and transaction hashes, 
and the block body, which consists of validated transactions.
A requested new transaction joins other combined blocks while network nodes vali -
date them through consensus protocols like Proof of Work or Stake. Block verification 
permits the blockchain to add the block while documenting the particular hash within 
the next block, thus creating an unchangeable linked chain. Any modification attempt

3.4 Machine learning model in the context of blockchain
Machine learning algorithms are data-driven models capable of learning patterns and 
making predictions without being explicitly programmed. In blockchain applications, 
these models contribute to intelligent decision-making in areas such as fraud detection, 
consensus optimization, and resource allocation. Logistic Regression (LR) is a widely 
used algorithm for binary classification, modeling the probability of outcomes using a 
sigmoid function. It is simple, interpretable, and effective for linearly separable data. 
The Support Vector Machine (SVM) identifies the optimal hyperplane for classification 
by maximizing the margin between classes, offering robustness in high-dimensional 
spaces, especially with an appropriate kernel based on Bayes’ theorem. Naïve Bayes (NB) 
assumes feature independence and performs efficiently in text classification and spam 
detection. Random Forest (RF), a bagging ensemble technique, combines multiple deci -
sion trees to improve prediction accuracy and reduce overfitting. LightGBM (LGB), a 
gradient-boosting Model, enhances efficiency by growing tree leaf-wise, offering faster 
training and better performance. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is a non-parametric algo -
rithm that classifies data points based on the majority class of their nearest neighbors. 
Despite its simplicity, it can be computationally intensive for large datasets. When inte -
grated with blockchain, these models can enhance data dependability and security while 
enabling decentralized intelligence.

4 Proposed blockchain enabled-internet of things model (BCE-IOT)
BCE-IoT utilises blockchain mechanisms and IoT systems to establish enhanced security 
protocols, comprehensive transparency capabilities, and deCentralized data exchange 
functionalities. Traditional IoT networks depend on centralized servers that create vul -
nerabilities to security attacks and both accessible data entry points and system single 
points of failure. The data exchanges between IoT devices use BCE-IoT to secure infor -
mation with blockchain features, including distributed ledger technology, blockchain 
cryptographic encryption, and smart contracts. Resource-constrained IoT devices ben -
efit from BCE-IoT because this solution utilises specific, lightweight consensus mecha -
nisms that enhance both efficiency and scalability. By combining blockchain technology 
with IoT, the proposed model establishes a reliable Framework that ensures safe, autono-
mous device-to-device operations in healthcare services, smart cities, and supply chain 
operations. The end-to-end data flow in BCE-IoT can be summarized as follows: IoT 
Sensor → Local Feature Extraction → ML Model Prediction → Prediction + SHAP 
Explanations → Hashed and stored on the Blockchain as a transaction. Each block thus 
serves as an immutable audit log of detections, ensuring integrity, transparency, and 
interpretability. This explicit flow highlights the interaction between the ML and block -
chain layers, bridging the gap between detection and secure logging.
Unlike earlier blockchain-enabled IDS models such as Blockchain-based Distrib -
uted Secure Decision Tree (BDSDT) and Blockchain-based Multi-Controller Software 
Defined Networking (BMC-SDN), which suffer from centralized elements, high compu -
tational costs, and a lack of transparency, BCE-IoT is designed with three key innova -
tions: (i) decentralized trust via blockchain consensus integrated with federated-style 
training, (ii) lightweight security mechanisms using Tiny Encryption Algorithm XXTEA, 
ECC tailored for IoT devices, and (iii) SHAP-based explainable AI integration for trans -
parent and interpretable intrusion detection. These contributions establish BCE-IoT as a 
more scalable and practical framework for IoT security.
4.1 Problem definition
The BCE-IoT Model has been developed to meet three main objectives among con -
ventional IoT platforms: addressing security weaknesses alongside data protection 
challenges, managing operations with centralization issues, and scalability problems. 
The traditional IoT architecture relies on cloud-based servers, which present multiple 
security challenges, data vulnerability, and central failure risks. The massive data out -
put from IoT devices creates data integrity problems, unauthorized access risks, and 
concerns about the reliability of third-party service providers. Conventional security 
measures often fall short in providing real-time, tamper-proof authentication and reli -
able data validation across interconnected devices. This limitation becomes critical in 
distributed environments, such as the IoT, where secure and continuous verification of 
device integrity and data authenticity is essential. The rapid growth in IoT device num -
bers creates problems for network expansion because it causes network congestion that 
drives up operational expenses. The BCE-IoT model implements blockchain technology,

Multiple customers can operate efficiently with secure decentralization since data pri -

ized authorities.

4.3 Blockchain enabled internet of things
Blockchain-enabled IoT is implemented with the following phases:
  • Device Registration and Authentication: All IoT devices are registered on the 
blockchain with unique cryptographic identities, ensuring secure access control and 
preventing unauthorised devices from joining the network.
  • Secure Data Transmission and Integrity: Blockchain data transmission becomes 
secure, and integrity is maintained because data remains immutable and shielded 
from unauthorised modifications.
  • Smart Contract Based Access Control: Smart contracts implement automated access 
controls, which validate transactions before blockchain storage to enable secure 
mergers between trustless and transparent operations.
  • Blockchain Consensus for Validation: The validation of shared transactions depends 
on blockchain consensus mechanisms, which consist of Byzantine Fault Tolerance 
consensus approaches to confirm that the ledger only contains valid information.
  • Privacy-Preserving Data Sharing: The sharing process of IoT data remains protected 
through zero-knowledge proofs combined with encryption methods to prevent the 
disclosure of confidential information.

The security within IoT ecosystems benefits from blockchain technology, which uses 
decentralized tamper-proof methods in the Blockchain- Enabled IoT Security Mecha -
nism, and traditional IoT networks remain exposed to critical cyber dangers because

device access, along with manipulation incidents. Locking security exists because block -
chain technology utilises distributed ledger technology with multiple nodes to create a 
transaction logging system, establishing transparency and immutable records that build 
trust throughout the system. Each IoT device obtains its cryptographic identity, which

and maintain a genuine device identity. Smart contracts implement automated secu -
rity protocols that enable predefined rules to regulate device interactions, substantially 
reducing security issues associated with human involvement. The data integrity capa -
bilities of blockchain ensure permanent storage of sensor-generated data in immutable 
ledgers that protect the data from unauthorized changes. Security barriers get enhanced 
through a machine learning and blockchain communication system, which enables the 
detection of anomalies, predictive threat analysis, and real-time threat responses. The 
decentralized security Model enhances the IoT network and flexibility. It works perfectly 
in critical infrastructure scenarios, such as healthcare and smart cities, with applications 
in industrial automation and supply chain management.

nology independently.

4.7 Proposed BCE-IoT model and machine learning algorithm working workflow
The proposed BCE-IoT and Machine Learning integrated model operates through a 
structured workflow to enhance trust management, authentication, and secure com -
munication in smart city IoT environments. Initially, each fog server generates a unique 
Fog ID (FID), and smart systems are assigned system IDs (SID) derived from a hash of 
the FID and system name. Each IoT node (T) within a smart system receives a Transac -
tion ID (TID), an ECC key pair, and a digital certificate containing identifiers, keys, and 
validity details. Once registered, the node’s behavioural and communication features are 
extracted and analysed using a pre-trained machine learning model to predict a trust 
score. The node is considered legitimate and allowed to proceed if the predicted trust 
score meets or exceeds a defined threshold. The node then encrypts its data using a 
lightweight XXTEA algorithm with a symmetric key, which is itself encrypted using the 
fog server’s public key via ECC. The encrypted data and key are sent to the fog server, 
which decrypts and verifies the credentials and trust score. Upon successful verification, 
the fog server forms a transaction and packages it into a new block. The server then 
performs a Proof-of-Work (PoW) process to validate the block, broadcasts it to other 
fog nodes, and integrates it into the blockchain ledger. The transaction is rejected if the 
trust score is below the threshold or if certificate verification. This hybrid workflow com-
bines the scalability and security of blockchain with the predictive and adaptive capa -
bilities of machine learning to deliver efficient, low-latency, and trustworthy IoT data 
management.
